blocks.md:
- Recognise and name the whole note, half note, quarter note, and eighth note (semibreve, minim, crotchet, and quaver) by sight, and match each to its rest.
- Explain how these four note values divide and combine (e.g. one half note equals two quarter notes).
- Identify the parts of a written note (note head, stem, flag) and apply the basic stem-direction rule.
blocks.label: In this lesson

blocks.md:
When you play a note on the piano, you make a choice that goes beyond *which* key to press. You also decide **how long to hold it down**. That length of time is called the note's **value**.

Note value simply means: how many beats does this note last?
**Beat:** A beat is one steady tick of a pulse, like the ticking of a clock or the consistent tap of a foot. Music is built on a steady stream of these equal ticks.

Think about the difference between a long, slow breath and a short quick breath. A slow breath lasts several seconds. A short one is over much quicker. Notes work the same way. Some notes ask you to hold the key down for many beats. Others ask you to press and release in much less time. Both are equally valid. The mix of long and short sounds is what gives music its rhythm.

1. Press middle C (the C roughly in the centre of the piano) and hold it down while you count slowly: one, two, three, four. That is a long note.
2. Now press middle C and count the same four beats, but press a new C on each beat: one, two, three, four. Those are much quicker notes.

Same key. Very different feel. That difference is all about note value.
blocks.title: Feel the difference at the piano

blocks.label: Middle C: the key used in the example above
A long note: C held (shown as four beats)
Short notes: four quicker Cs in a row

blocks.md: Written music uses different note symbols to tell you exactly how long each sound lasts. Once you can read those symbols, the page tells you not just *what* to play but *how long* to play it. That is why note values are one of the first things every musician learns.

A steady beat does not have to be fast. It just has to be **even**. Try tapping your foot at a comfortable walking pace. That tap is your beat. Everything in this lesson is measured against a pulse just like that.

Before moving on, try this. Tap a steady beat with your foot. With one hand, press middle C and hold it for four taps. Then try pressing C on every single tap. Notice how the music feels completely different even though the beat you tap with your foot stays the same. You have just experienced two different note values.

items.prompt: What does a note's value tell you?
items.explain: Note value tells you the duration of a note, meaning how many beats you hold it. Which key to press is shown by the note's position on the stave, and loudness is shown by separate markings.
options: Which key to press on the piano
How loud to play the note
How many beats to hold the note down
How fast to tap your foot

items.prompt: A beat is a steady, even pulse, like the ticking of a clock.
items.explain: Correct. A beat is one steady tick in an ongoing, even pulse. Music is measured in these equal, regular ticks.

items.prompt: You press middle C and hold it for four beats. Then you press middle C four times, once on each beat. What is different between these two actions?
items.explain: The pitch (middle C) stays the same both times, and the beat stays steady. What changes is the note value: the first is one long note lasting four beats, and the second is four short notes each lasting one beat.
options: The note value is different: one is a long note, the other is four short notes
The beat speeds up the second time
Nothing is different; they sound exactly the same

blocks.md: A **note value** tells you how long to hold a sound. Think of it as a time instruction printed on the page. There are four note values you will use in almost every piece you ever play. We will cover these one at a time, from the longest to the shortest.
The **whole note**, also called a *semibreve*, lasts **4 beats**. It is the longest of the four values. On the page it looks like a small open oval, with no stem attached.

blocks.caption: A whole note on Middle C. The open oval with no stem lasts a full 4 beats.

blocks.md: Find **Middle C** (the C nearest the middle of your piano). Press it and count out loud: **1, 2, 3, 4**. Keep the key held down for the whole count. That is one whole note.
blocks.title: Try it at the piano

blocks.label: Middle C (hold for 4 beats)
Whole note: Middle C held for 4 beats

blocks.md: The **half note**, also called a *minim*, lasts **2 beats**. That is exactly half a whole note. It looks like an open oval **with a stem** attached to its side.

blocks.caption: Two half notes: Middle C (2 beats) then E (2 beats). Each open oval with a stem lasts 2 beats.

blocks.md: Press **Middle C** and count: **1, 2**. Release, then press **E** (two white keys to the right of C) and count: **1, 2**. You have just played two half notes, filling the same time as one whole note.
blocks.title: Try it at the piano

blocks.label: C then E, two beats each
A half note held for 2 beats: C, then E

blocks.md: The **quarter note**, also called a *crotchet*, lasts **1 beat**. It is the note value most often used for a steady pulse. It looks like a **filled-in (solid) oval with a stem**. Two quarter notes equal one half note. Four quarter notes equal one whole note.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
C D E F
blocks.caption: Four quarter notes: C, D, E, F. Each solid oval with a stem lasts exactly 1 beat.

blocks.md: Starting on **Middle C**, play the next four white notes one at a time: **C, D, E, F**. Say each number as you press: **1, 2, 3, 4**. One key per beat. Those are four quarter notes.
blocks.title: Try it at the piano

blocks.label: C D E F, one beat each
Four quarter notes: C D E F

blocks.md: The **eighth note**, also called a *quaver*, lasts **half a beat**. Two eighth notes fit inside one quarter note. It looks like a filled-in oval with a stem **and a small curved flag** attached to the top of the stem. When two or more eighth notes appear in a row, their flags are often joined by a horizontal beam instead, but they are still eighth notes.

blocks.caption: Eight eighth notes beamed in pairs. Each lasts half a beat, so two eighth notes fill one beat.

blocks.md: Play **C and D** evenly in the space of one beat. Count: **1-and**. The word 'and' lands exactly halfway through the beat. C on '1', D on 'and'. That quick, even pair is two eighth notes.
blocks.title: Try it at the piano

blocks.label: C and D as an eighth note pair
Two eighth notes: C then D (one beat total)

blocks.md: A useful counting trick: say '1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and' to keep track of eighth notes. Each number is a beat. Each 'and' is the halfway point between two beats.

blocks.text: All Four Values Side by Side

blocks.md:
Here is how the four values relate to each other:

- **Whole note** = 4 beats
- **Half note** = 2 beats (2 half notes fit in 1 whole note)
- **Quarter note** = 1 beat (4 quarter notes fit in 1 whole note)
- **Eighth note** = half a beat (8 eighth notes fit in 1 whole note)

blocks.caption: Bar 1: one whole note. Bar 2: two half notes. Bar 3: four quarter notes. Bar 4: eight eighth notes. All bars last exactly 4 beats.

blocks.md: You might spot two new things on the staves above: the two numbers stacked at the very start (the **time signature**) and the short vertical lines that split the notes into groups (**bar lines**). You do not need to understand these yet. They are simply here to keep the beats organised. We will cover both properly in upcoming lessons. For now, just focus on the note values themselves.
Every bar above lasts exactly 4 beats. The notes just divide that time into bigger or smaller slices. This is how rhythm works.

Sit at your piano and try this sequence on **Middle C** only:

1. Hold C for 4 counts (whole note).
2. Play C twice, 2 counts each (two half notes).
3. Play C four times, 1 count each (four quarter notes).
4. Play C eight times, counting '1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and' (eight eighth notes).

Keep a steady speed throughout. Notice how each line contains more notes but has the same pulse.

items.prompt: How many beats does a half note last?
items.explain: A half note lasts 2 beats. It is half the length of a whole note (4 beats) and twice the length of a quarter note (1 beat).

items.prompt: Which note value has a filled-in oval, a stem, and a flag?
items.explain: The eighth note has a filled-in oval, a stem, and a flag (or a beam when grouped). The whole note has no stem, the half note has an open oval with a stem, and the quarter note has a filled-in oval with a stem but no flag.

items.prompt: Four quarter notes last the same total time as one whole note.
items.explain: Yes. A whole note lasts 4 beats and a quarter note lasts 1 beat, so four quarter notes add up to exactly 4 beats, the same as one whole note.

blocks.text: Anatomy of a Note: Head, Stem, and Flag

blocks.md: Every note you see written on a page is built from up to three simple parts. Learning to spot these parts is how you instantly read a note's value at a glance. Let's learn each part now.

**The note head** is the oval shape that sits on or between the lines of the stave. The stave is the set of five horizontal lines on which music is written. The note head's position on the stave tells you the pitch (how high or low the note sounds). Its appearance, open or filled, tells you part of the note's value.

**The stem** is the thin vertical line attached to the note head. It points either up or down. Not every note value has a stem.

**The flag** is the curved tail attached to the top or bottom of the stem. Only one of our four note values carries a flag.
How notes look on the stave determines it's value.

blocks.text: How the parts combine for each value

blocks.md: Here is what each of the four note values looks like and which parts it uses.

blocks.caption: The whole note: an open, hollow note head. No stem. No flag. It lasts four beats.
The half note: an open, hollow note head with a stem. No flag. It lasts two beats.
The quarter note: a filled, solid note head with a stem. No flag. It lasts one beat.
The eighth note: a filled, solid note head with a stem and a flag. It lasts half a beat.

blocks.md:
Look at the half note and the quarter note side by side. Both have a stem. The only difference is the note head: the half note's head is hollow (open inside), and the quarter note's head is filled (solid black). That single visual detail doubles the value. An open head means the note lasts longer.

Now compare the quarter note and the eighth note. Both have a filled head. The only difference is the flag on the eighth note's stem. That one curved line cuts the value in half.
blocks.title: Spot the difference

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
C4 C2 C C/2
blocks.caption: All four values on the same pitch (C4, middle C): whole note, half note, quarter note, eighth note. Watch how the head and stem change.

blocks.md:
Here is a quick reference for the four values and their parts:

- **Whole note:** open head, no stem, no flag
- **Half note:** open head, stem, no flag
- **Quarter note:** filled head, stem, no flag
- **Eighth note:** filled head, stem, flag

A useful memory trick: the more parts a note has, the shorter its value. The whole note has just a head and lasts longest. The eighth note has a head, a stem, and a flag, and lasts the shortest of the four.

items.prompt: A note has a filled (solid) head, a stem, and a flag. Which note value is it?
items.explain: The eighth note is the only one of the four values with all three parts: a filled head, a stem, and a flag. The quarter note has a filled head and a stem but no flag.

items.prompt: A half note and a quarter note look identical except that the half note's note head is open (hollow) and the quarter note's is filled (solid).
items.explain: Correct. Both the half note and the quarter note have a stem and no flag. The only visual difference is the note head: open for the half note, filled for the quarter note.

items.prompt: Which note value has NO stem and NO flag?
items.explain: The whole note is just an open note head with nothing else attached. It has no stem and no flag, and it lasts the longest of the four values.

blocks.md: Every note with a stem (that is, every note except a whole note) follows a simple rule about which way the stem points. This rule exists purely to keep written music tidy and easy to read. Once you know it, you will spot it instantly on any page of sheet music.

First, a quick reminder about the stave. The stave is the set of five horizontal lines that music is written on. The lines are counted from the bottom upward: line 1 at the bottom, line 3 in the middle, line 5 at the top. **Line 3 is the middle line**, and that is the key reference point for this rule.

blocks.caption: The stave has five lines. Line 3 is the middle line, right in the centre.

blocks.md:
**The Stem-Direction Rule**

- If a note sits **on or above** the middle line (line 3), its stem points **downward**.
- If a note sits **below** the middle line (line 3), its stem points **upward**.
Stems grow inward toward the centre of the stave rather than flying off the edges. This keeps everything compact and easy on the eye.

blocks.text: Example 1: A note below the middle line (stem points up)

blocks.md: The note D sits below the middle line of the treble clef stave. Because it is below the middle line, its stem points **upward**. Here it is written out so you can see it clearly.

blocks.caption: D4 (below the middle line in the treble clef). Notice the stem rises upward from the right side of the note head.

blocks.md: Now find that note on your keyboard. D4 is the white key sitting between the group of two black keys, just to the right of middle C.

blocks.label: D4: a note below the middle line. Stem points up.
Hear D4

blocks.text: Example 2: A note on or above the middle line (stem points down)

blocks.md: The note B sits on the middle line of the treble clef stave. Because it is on the middle line, its stem points **downward**. You can see the stem hanging below the note head in the example below.

blocks.caption: B4 (on the middle line in the treble clef). Notice the stem drops downward from the left side of the note head.

blocks.md: Find B4 on your keyboard. It is the white key immediately to the left of the group of two black keys, sitting just above middle C on the stave.

blocks.label: B4: a note above the middle line. Stem points down.
Hear B4

blocks.md: Here are D4 and B4 written one after the other. Look at the stems before reading on. D4 stem goes up, B4 stem goes down. The pattern is clear straight away.
blocks.title: Both notes together: spot the stem directions

blocks.caption: D4 (stem up) followed by B4 (stem down). One note below the middle line, one on it.

blocks.label: Hear D4 then B4

blocks.md: When a note sits **exactly on** the middle line (line 3, which is B4 in the treble clef), the convention is to point the stem downward. If you are ever unsure, ask yourself: is the note on or above the middle? If yes, stem goes down.

A small detail worth knowing: when the stem points **up**, it grows from the **right side** of the note head. When it points **down**, it grows from the **left side**. You do not need to memorise this right now. It will become natural as you read more music.

Sit at your piano. Play D4 (below middle line, stem up) and then B4 (above middle line, stem down) one at a time. Each time you play a note, say out loud whether its stem on the stave points up or down. Then glance back at the notation examples above and check yourself.

items.prompt: A note is written below the middle line of the stave. Which way does its stem point?
items.explain: Notes below the middle line have stems that point upward. This keeps the stem growing toward the centre of the stave, which makes the music easier to read.
options: It depends on the note's name

items.prompt: A note sitting exactly on the middle line of the stave should have its stem pointing downward.
items.explain: Correct. A note on the middle line is treated the same as a note above it: the stem points downward. The rule is 'on or above the middle line, stem goes down'.

items.prompt: Look at D4 and B4 on the stave above. Which note has its stem pointing upward?
items.explain: D4 sits below the middle line, so its stem points upward. B4 sits above the middle line, so its stem points downward.
options: B4, because it is above the middle line
D4, because it is below the middle line

blocks.title: Check your understanding: The Stem-Direction Rule

blocks.md:
Every note value fits neatly inside a larger one. This is not random. The whole system is built on one simple rule: **each value is exactly half the length of the one above it**.

That means you can always swap one longer note for two shorter ones of equal total length, or join shorter notes together to make a longer one. This is the heartbeat of rhythm.

- 1 whole note (4 beats)
- = 2 half notes (2 beats each)
- = 4 quarter notes (1 beat each)
- = 8 eighth notes (half a beat each)

Every row lasts exactly 4 beats in total. Only the number of pieces changes.
blocks.title: The relationship tree, from longest to shortest

blocks.caption: One whole note: 4 beats, one note fills the whole bar.
Two half notes: still 4 beats, now split into two equal halves.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C C C C
blocks.caption: Four quarter notes: still 4 beats, one note per beat.
Eight eighth notes: still 4 beats, two notes per beat.

blocks.md: **The golden rule:** however many notes you use, the total always adds up to the same number of beats. The bar never stretches or shrinks.

You do not have to fill a bar with identical notes. You can mix values freely, as long as the beats add up correctly. This is where rhythm starts to feel musical.

Here is a simple, concrete example to make this real.

- 1 half note = 2 beats
- 1 quarter note = 1 beat
- 1 quarter note = 1 beat
- Total: 2 + 1 + 1 = **4 beats**. The bar is exactly full.
blocks.title: One half note plus two quarter notes equals four beats

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C2 C C
blocks.caption: A half note (2 beats) followed by two quarter notes (1 beat each). Count: 1-2, 3, 4.

blocks.md: Count out loud as you look at it: **1, 2** (hold for the half note), then **3** (first quarter note), then **4** (second quarter note). Notice how the half note takes up two counts on its own.

**Tap before you play.** Place one hand on your knee. Tap once and hold for the half note (counts 1 and 2), then tap twice more, one tap per quarter note (counts 3 and 4). Say the numbers out loud. Get the feeling in your body before you touch the keys.

**Step 1: Tap it on your knee.** Pat your knee steadily and count: 1, 2, 3, 4. Keep going until it feels even.

Now add the rhythm on top:

- Tap and hold through counts 1 and 2 (the half note).
- Tap once on count 3 (first quarter note).
- Tap once on count 4 (second quarter note).

Repeat four times. Say the numbers out loud each time.

**Step 2: Play it on any comfortable key.** Choose any white key that feels easy to reach. Middle C (the C in the middle of your keyboard) is a good choice.

Play the same pattern:

- Press and hold for counts 1 and 2.
- Play once on count 3.
- Play once on count 4.

Keep the pulse steady. You are not playing a melody yet, just one note with a rhythm. That is perfect.

blocks.label: Hear the rhythm: half note then two quarter notes on middle C (played as a sequence)

blocks.md:
Once that feels comfortable, try another combination that also adds up to four beats:

- 4 quarter notes (1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4)
- 1 whole note (4 beats, hold the key down and count slowly to four)
- 2 half notes (2 + 2 = 4)

Each of these fills the bar in a completely different way. That variety is exactly what makes rhythm interesting.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C C C C | C2 C2 | C4
blocks.caption: Three different ways to fill a 4-beat bar: four quarter notes, two half notes, one whole note. Same number of beats, very different feels.

items.prompt: You have one half note in a 4-beat bar. How many beats are left to fill?
items.explain: A half note lasts 2 beats. A full bar has 4 beats. 4 minus 2 leaves 2 beats still to fill.

items.prompt: Which combination exactly fills a 4-beat bar?
items.explain: One half note (2 beats) plus two quarter notes (1 beat each) gives 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 beats. That fills the bar exactly. The other options add up to 5, 3, and 5 beats respectively.
options: One whole note and one quarter note
One half note and two quarter notes
Two half notes and one quarter note

items.prompt: One whole note lasts the same total time as four quarter notes.
items.explain: A whole note lasts 4 beats. Four quarter notes, at 1 beat each, also total 4 beats. They are equal in length, just written as different numbers of notes.

blocks.md:
You have now seen four note values. Each one has a equivalent **rest**.

A rest is a moment of **silence**. It lasts for exactly the same number of beats as its matching note. A whole rest lasts four beats of silence. A half rest lasts two. A quarter rest lasts one. An eighth rest lasts half a beat.

Rests are not empty gaps. They are instructions. They tell you to be silent for a precise amount of time. Counting them carefully is just as important as counting the notes.
**The golden rule:** a rest = silence for the same number of beats as its matching note. The music keeps moving, you just do not play.

blocks.text: The Four Rests on the Stave

blocks.md: Here are all four rests written on a stave. Look carefully at their shapes and where they sit.

blocks.caption: Whole rest (4 beats): a filled rectangle that hangs below the fourth line of the stave.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
z2 z z
blocks.caption: Half rest (2 beats) followed by two quarter rests (1 beat each): the half rest is a filled rectangle sitting on top of the middle line; the quarter rest is a zigzag symbol.
Eight eighth rests (half a beat each) filling one bar of 4/4: each looks like a small curved symbol, similar to a numeral 7.

blocks.md:
- **Whole rest (4 beats):** a solid filled rectangle hanging *below* a stave line. Think of it as a heavy block that droops down.
- **Half rest (2 beats):** a solid filled rectangle sitting *on top of* a stave line. Think of it as a hat resting on the line.
- **Quarter rest (1 beat):** a zigzag symbol. It is the most elaborate of the four shapes.
- **Eighth rest (half a beat):** a small curved symbol that looks a little like a stylised numeral 7 with a dot.
blocks.title: A quick guide to the four rest shapes

blocks.md: **Half note or whole rest? A simple trick.** The half rest sits **on** the line like a hat. The whole rest hangs heavy **below** the line. If you can remember that the whole rest is longer and heavier, you will remember which one sits on the line and which one hangs from it.

A common mistake is to rush through a rest as if it were nothing. Try counting aloud while you listen to this short rhythm. It contains notes and rests. Keep counting steadily all the way through, even when you hear silence.

blocks.label: A one-bar quarter note pattern with a rest on beat 3: C, E, silence, G

blocks.md: Did you notice the gap before the G? That silence on beat 3 is a quarter rest. The beat still happens inside your head, you just do not play anything on it.

blocks.text: Rests in a Full Bar of 4/4

blocks.md: Here is a four-beat bar mixing quarter notes and a quarter rest. Read it before you try the task below.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C E z G
blocks.caption: Four beats: C (beat 1), E (beat 2), quarter rest (beat 3, silence), G (beat 4).

blocks.label: The three notes used in the pattern: C4, E4, and G4

blocks.md:
**Clap and lift: feel the rest in your body.**

1. Set a slow, steady pulse, about one beat per second. Count "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud a few times to lock in the tempo (speed).
2. Now follow the pattern above. Clap on beats 1, 2, and 4. On beat 3, lift both hands up and away, say "rest" aloud, and stay silent for exactly one beat before clapping again on beat 4.
3. Repeat the pattern four times without stopping. Keep counting all the way through.
4. When the clapping feels natural, sit at the piano. Play C4 on beat 1, E4 on beat 2, lift your hand on beat 3, and play G4 on beat 4. Use the keyboard diagram above to find the notes.
5. Finally, try replacing beat 1 with a rest as well: silence, E4, silence, G4. You are now holding two separate silences inside one bar.

**Watch out for rushing.** Most beginners shorten rests and play the next note too early. Say the beat number aloud on every beat, including rests. Hearing your own voice on beat 3 will stop you from jumping ahead.

items.prompt: How many beats of silence does a half rest last?
items.explain: A half rest lasts 2 beats, exactly the same as a half note. It looks like a filled rectangle sitting on top of a stave line.

items.prompt: The whole rest hangs below a stave line, while the half rest sits on top of a stave line.
items.explain: Correct. The whole rest droops below the line and the half rest perches on top of it, like a hat. This difference in position is the easiest way to tell them apart.

items.prompt: In the pattern C, E, rest, G (one beat each), which beat is silent?
items.explain: The rest appears third in the pattern, so it falls on beat 3. The beat still counts in your head; you simply do not play anything on it.

blocks.text: Putting It Together at the Piano

blocks.md:
You have met all four note values and their matching rests. Now it is time to use them.

In this section you will take a short four-bar rhythm, count it aloud, clap it, and then play it on a single note: Middle C. One note, all your attention on the rhythm. That is exactly how professional musicians learn a tricky passage.
**Why one note?** When you remove the job of finding different pitches, your brain is free to focus entirely on rhythm. This is a real practice technique, not a shortcut.

Here is the rhythm written on a stave. Every note is Middle C. The time signature is 4/4, which means there are four beats in every bar. Count those beats as "1, 2, 3, 4" and then start again at 1 for each new bar.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C4 | C2 C2 | C C C z | C C2 C
blocks.caption: Four bars on Middle C using a whole note, half notes, quarter notes, and a quarter rest. Every notehead sits on the Middle C ledger line below the treble stave.

blocks.md:
Here is what each bar contains:

- **Bar 1:** One whole note. It lasts all four beats by itself.
- **Bar 2:** Two half notes. Each lasts two beats: one half note on beats 1 and 2, another on beats 3 and 4.
- **Bar 3:** Three quarter notes, then one quarter rest. One beat each. The rest is silence on beat 4.
- **Bar 4:** One quarter note, one half note, one quarter note. Beats: 1, then 2 and 3 together, then 4.

Before you touch the piano, say the beat numbers out loud while you follow the notation above. Keep a steady, slow pace, like a ticking clock.

Say it like this:

**Bar 1:** "1 - 2 - 3 - 4" (one long sound, all four beats)

**Bar 2:** "1 - 2 - 3 - 4" (new sound on 1, new sound on 3)

**Bar 3:** "1 - 2 - 3 - rest" (say "rest" out loud on beat 3, no sound)

**Bar 4:** "1 - 2 - 3 - 4" (sound on 1, hold through 2 and 3, new sound on 4)

Repeat this two or three times until it feels natural at your chosen speed.
blocks.title: Counting the rhythm aloud

blocks.md: Set a timer or use a metronome at around 60 beats per minute (one beat per second). Slow is good. Slow is how accuracy is built.

Now clap the rhythm while you continue counting aloud. Clap on every note. On the rest in bar 3, open your hands instead of clapping, and say "rest" as before.

This step connects the written symbols to a physical action. It is much easier to transfer to the keys once your hands already know the shape of the rhythm.
Clap and count the four bars three times in a row without stopping. If you stumble, slow down further rather than going back to the beginning. Keep the pulse going.
Middle C is the C closest to the middle of your piano keyboard. It sits just to the left of the group of two black keys near the centre of the instrument. Use your right hand thumb (finger 1).

blocks.label: Middle C on the keyboard
Middle C (the only pitch you will play)

blocks.md:
Keep counting aloud and play Middle C every time a note starts. Hold each key down for exactly as long as the note value tells you, then release it on the rest or when the next note begins.

Here is what to listen for as you play:

blocks.label: Bar 1: Whole note (4 beats)
Bar 2: Two half notes (2 beats each)
Bar 3: Quarter note, quarter note, quarter note, rest (1 beat each)
Bar 4: Quarter note, half note, quarter note

blocks.md: **Watch for this common slip:** holding a whole note or half note for too long, or not long enough. Count every beat out loud. If your mouth keeps counting while your finger stays down, the note length will almost always be correct.
Play the full four bars from start to finish, counting aloud the whole time. Aim for three clean run-throughs in a row. When you can do that at 60 bpm, try nudging the speed up to 72 bpm.

blocks.text: Why This Matters for Every Piece You Will Ever Play

blocks.md:
Every single piece of music you will ever play is built from the same four note values you just used. A beginner piece and a Beethoven sonata both live on the same foundation: whole notes, half notes, quarter notes, and eighth notes, mixed with rests.

When you can recognise a note value the instant you see it, and feel its length in your body without counting aloud, reading music becomes much, much easier. That instant recognition is a skill, and like any skill it grows with practice each day.

You have just taken the first step.

**The big idea:** Note values tell you how long to hold each sound. Rests tell you how long to stay silent. Together they create rhythm, and rhythm is the engine that drives all music forward. Recognise note values quickly and you hold the key to reading any piece of music on the page.

items.prompt: In the rhythm above, bar 1 contains a whole note. How many beats do you count while holding that single note down?
items.explain: A whole note lasts for 4 beats. In 4/4 time that fills the entire bar on its own. You count '1, 2, 3, 4' while keeping the key held down.

items.prompt: When you reach the quarter rest in bar 3, you should lift your finger and stay silent for one beat before playing again.
items.explain: A quarter rest means one full beat of silence. Lifting your finger and saying 'rest' aloud on that beat keeps your counting steady and makes the silence audible, which is just as important as the notes around it.

blocks.md: Every piece you will ever play is built from the note and rest values you have just learned. When you sit at the piano and read a simple melody, the note heads tell you *which* key to press, and the note values tell you *how long* to hold it. If a whole note appears, you press the key and let it ring for four full beats. If a quarter note appears, you move on after one beat. Rests are just as important: a quarter rest means you lift your hand and let silence fill that beat. Even in the very first beginner pieces in your repertoire, you will find whole notes, half notes, quarter notes, and eighth notes appearing within the first few bars. Recognising them instantly means you can focus on the music rather than stopping to count.

- **Note value**: how long a musical sound lasts, measured in beats
- **Rest**: a moment of silence with its own specific length, just like a note
- **Whole note (semibreve)**: a note that lasts four beats; written as a hollow oval with no stem
- **Half note (minim)**: a note that lasts two beats; written as a hollow oval with a stem
- **Quarter note (crotchet)**: a note that lasts one beat; written as a filled oval with a stem
- **Eighth note (quaver)**: a note that lasts half a beat; written as a filled oval with a stem and a flag (or joined to neighbours by a beam)
- **Whole rest (semibreve rest)**: a rest that lasts four beats, or a whole bar in simple time
- **Half rest (minim rest)**: a rest that lasts two beats
- **Quarter rest (crotchet rest)**: a rest that lasts one beat
- **Eighth rest (quaver rest)**: a rest that lasts half a beat
- **Note head**: the oval part of a written note, which sits on a line or space of the stave
- **Stem**: the thin vertical line attached to the note head
- **Flag**: the curved line added to a stem to halve the note's value (one flag = eighth note)
- **Beam**: a thick horizontal bar that joins two or more flagged notes together for easier reading
- **Stem-direction rule**: stems point up when the note head sits below the middle line of the stave, and down when it sits on or above the middle line
- **Beat**: the steady, repeating pulse that runs through a piece of music
- **Bar (measure)**: a small group of beats marked off by vertical lines on the stave

- A **note value** tells you how long to hold a sound; a **rest value** tells you how long to stay silent.
- The four core note values are: whole note (4 beats), half note (2 beats), quarter note (1 beat), and eighth note (half a beat).
- Each value is exactly **half** the one above it: one whole note equals two half notes, one half note equals two quarter notes, one quarter note equals two eighth notes.
- A note is built from three parts: the **head** (which note to play), the **stem** (points up or down by rule), and, for eighth notes, a **flag**.
- Flags can be replaced by a **beam** when two or more eighth notes appear next to each other.
- Every note value has a matching **rest symbol** that lasts the same number of beats.
- Silence is musical: rests shape rhythm just as much as the notes themselves do.

items.prompt: A half note lasts for how many beats in 4/4 time?
items.explain: A half note lasts for 2 beats. It takes two half notes to fill a whole note, which lasts 4 beats.

items.prompt: Two quarter notes together are worth the same total length as one half note.
items.explain: Correct. A half note lasts 2 beats and a quarter note lasts 1 beat, so two quarter notes add up to exactly 2 beats, the same as one half note.

items.prompt: An open (hollow) note head means a longer note; a filled-in (solid) head means a shorter one. Which part of a note gives you this first clue to its length?
items.explain: The note head's shape is the first clue to a note's value: an open (hollow) head is a half or whole note, while a filled (solid) head is a quarter note or shorter. The stem and any flags then refine the exact value.

items.prompt: A whole rest looks like a filled rectangle hanging DOWN from a line on the stave. What kind of rest hangs UP from a line instead?
items.explain: The half rest is a filled rectangle that sits ON TOP of a line, as if it is a hat. The whole rest hangs below a line, like a heavy block falling down.

items.prompt: A note sits below the middle line of the stave. According to the stem-direction rule, which way should its stem point?
items.explain: When a note sits below the middle line of the stave, its stem points upward. When a note sits above the middle line, the stem points downward. This keeps the notation tidy and easy to read.
options: It does not have a stem
Either direction, it makes no difference
